Oedipus Rex. Sophocles' masterpiece, performed around 429 BCE, and perhaps the most perfectly structured tragedy ever written. It examines fate, knowledge, and the question of whether any of us truly control our own lives. A king discovers through relentless investigation that he has unwittingly become the very thing he set out to destroy.

Oedipus rules Thebes. He solved the Sphinx's riddle years ago and won both the throne and the hand of Jocasta, the widowed queen. Now, a plague is ravaging the city. Oedipus vows to find and punish the murderer of the previous king, Laius, believing that justice will lift the curse.

He interrogates the blind prophet Tiresias. He pursues witnesses. Slowly, piece by piece, the truth emerges. Oedipus himself is the murderer. Years ago, trying to escape a prophecy that he would kill his father and marry his mother, he was fleeing Thebes when he encountered a man at a crossroads. They fought. He won. The man was Laius.

And the woman he married to escape that prophecy? She was his mother, Jocasta.

The play's tragic irony cuts deeper than any blade. Oedipus didn't fail because he was helpless. He failed because he tried to escape his fate so deliberately, so intelligently, that his very effort led him straight into it. Knowledge itself becomes his punishment. Each question he asks brings him closer to ruin, yet he cannot stop asking.

When Jocasta learns the truth, she hangs herself. Oedipus blinds himself and goes into exile, carrying with him the weight of his unwanted knowledge. The play asks: if you learned you were fundamentally corrupted, could you live with that knowledge? Sophocles suggests the answer is almost unbearable.
